clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive dyserythropoietic anaemia most often caused by biallelic mutations in CDAN1 (codanin-1) or in C15orf41
Presents with a moderate macrocytic anaemia, ineffective erythropoiesis, and secondary iron overload
The hallmark marrow finding is erythroblasts joined by thin internuclear chromatin bridges together with a spongy, 'Swiss-cheese' heterochromatin appearance on electron microscopy
Splenomegaly and intermittent jaundice reflect the haemolytic component of ineffective erythropoiesis
Some patients have associated skeletal anomalies, particularly of the hands and feet, and nail changes
Reticulocyte count is inappropriately low for the degree of anaemia, indicating ineffective marrow output
Interferon alpha has been reported to improve the anaemia in CDA I, distinguishing its management from other subtypes
Iron loading occurs even without transfusion because chronic ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin and drives excessive gut iron absorption
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia type I results from biallelic loss of function of codanin-1 (or its partner C15orf41), proteins involved in nuclear-envelope and chromatin regulation during erythroid maturation. Defective chromatin condensation and abnormal nuclear division produce dysplastic erythroblasts with internuclear bridges and spongy heterochromatin, and many maturing red-cell precursors are destroyed within the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis). The resulting anaemia and low hepcidin state drive inappropriate iron absorption and progressive tissue iron overload, which becomes a major long-term complication.
additionalDifferentials: Megaloblastic anaemia from B12 or folate deficiency
Chronic haemolytic anaemia of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and reticulocyte count showing macrocytic anaemia with inappropriately low reticulocytes
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine looking for internuclear bridges and dyserythropoiesis
Electron microscopy of erythroblasts for the spongy heterochromatin pattern
Iron studies including ferritin and transferrin saturation to assess overload
Genetic testing for CDAN1 and C15orf41 mutations
Haemolysis markers (bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin) and exclusion of thalassaemia and B12/folate deficiency
redFlags: Symptomatic or progressive iron overload with cardiac, hepatic, or endocrine dysfunction
Severe anaemia in the neonatal or fetal period requiring transfusion
Worsening cytopenias or marrow dysplasia raising concern for an alternative diagnosis
Features of decompensated haemolysis such as aplastic crisis after parvovirus infection
reference.prognosis: Many patients maintain a moderate, non-transfusion-dependent anaemia, and interferon alpha can raise haemoglobin, but iron overload accumulates over decades and, if unmonitored, drives the main morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Attributing iron overload solely to transfusion and missing the intrinsic ineffective-erythropoiesis mechanism
Confusing dyserythropoietic marrow with myelodysplasia and pursuing inappropriate treatment
Relying on iron studies alone and delaying genetic confirmation
Failing to screen for and treat iron loading in patients who are not transfused
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Interferon alpha is the disease-specific therapy in type I disease and can raise haemoglobin and reduce transfusion requirement
Iron chelation with deferasirox, deferiprone or desferrioxamine for the progressive iron overload that accrues from hepcidin suppression independent of transfusion
Provide folic acid supplementation to support ineffective erythropoiesis
Reserve leucodepleted, phenotype-matched transfusion for symptomatic anaemia, and consider splenectomy for the haemolytic component
Monitor ferritin and hepatic and cardiac iron by MRI, with surveillance for pigment gallstones
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive CDAN1/C15orf41 inheritance and test at-risk relatives
Refer to specialist haematology and clinical genetics and consider allogeneic stem cell transplantation in severe cases
